claims.claim: 3. Any file the reader cannot read that mentions the verifier refuses outright rather than reading as clean
claims.verdict: DISSENTED - this is the material finding
claims.evidence:
The rule is `if not graded and "scripts/verify.py" in text`. It is scoped per file and gated on that file having yielded NO graded step at all. A file the reader can only PARTLY read does not refuse, and the file that matters is exactly such a file. Two constructions, both executed against a throwaway copy of the real tree, both passing the entire suite with `unretained` returning `[]`, `graded` still 4 and `tried` still 12:
(A) append to `.github/workflows/verify.yml` a third job whose `steps:` key carries a trailing comment - `    steps:  # run the verifier` - followed by a bare `- run: python scripts/verify.py` and no retention step. `steps_of` finds its start line by `line.rstrip().endswith("steps:")`, which a trailing comment defeats, so the job yields zero steps. verify.yml's own two verify steps keep `graded` at 2 for that file, so the unreadable rule never fires.
(B) the same third job written as `    steps: [{run: python scripts/verify.py}]`, a YAML flow sequence. Same result.
Both shapes were confirmed to be valid YAML that parses to exactly the structure the reader expects: `yaml.safe_load` returns `{'steps': [{'run': 'python scripts/verify.py'}]}` for each, identical to the block form. A trailing comment after a mapping key is ordinary YAML and GitHub Actions accepts it. Control (D): the same hidden job placed ALONE in a new file does trip the rule, and (E) a composite action under `.github/actions` whose text spells `scripts/verify.py` trips it too - so the rule works exactly where the file has nothing else to grade, and fails exactly where a real workflow would put a new job. The rule the claim describes is 'any file it cannot read'; the rule the code implements is 'a file in which it found no verify step at all'. Those differ in the one direction that matters for a catch-all.

claims.claim: 4. The guard refuses every verify step in .github/workflows that keeps only an exit code
claims.evidence: Beyond claim 3's hidden steps, five further shapes pass `unretained` while removing the property it names, all executed rather than read off the source. `continue-on-error: True` and `continue-on-error: TRUE` on the retention step: PASS. Both are YAML booleans; the guard tests `"true" in (keys_of(keeper).get("continue-on-error"), settings.get("continue-on-error"))`, an exact string membership against a tuple, so any spelling but lowercase `true` escapes. `continue-on-error: ${{ true }}` and any templated truthy such as `${{ github.event_name == 'push' }}`: PASS. The same three spellings at job level: PASS. Quoted `'true'` and `"true"` are correctly refused, via `_unquoted`. This is the second witness's own N15/N9 finding surviving in a different spelling: the repair made `if-no-files-found: error` the load-bearing runtime enforcement, and `continue-on-error` is what neuters it. `branch-retirement.yml:65` already carries `continue-on-error: true`, so the shape is in the house vocabulary. Separately, two `if:` keys on one step with the defective one written first: PASS, because `mapping_at` builds a dict and the later key wins. GitHub rejects duplicate mapping keys, so that one is theoretical. Ungraded routes remain as the second witness described them and I re-confirmed two: a composite action whose text never spells `scripts/verify.py` and is called by `uses: ./.github/actions/verify` (PASS), and `run: make verify` (PASS).

claims.claim: 6. No NEW legal spelling is over-refused
claims.evidence: Nine, each executed. Conservative rather than dangerous, but each forecloses a shape a future author would reach for, and two produce a message that misnames the defect. (i) `if:` written as a folded scalar over two lines. (ii) `if-no-files-found: error  # a trailing comment` - the repair for N19 taught `mapping_at` to skip whole comment LINES, but `PAIR` still swallows a trailing comment into the value, so the mirror of the defect it fixed is now live. (iii) the same for `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}  # keep records`. (iv) a `with:` block written in flow style. (v) a whole keeper step written in flow style. (vi) `path: ${{runner.temp}}/obs.json` without the inner spaces. (vii) `--observe '$RUNNER_TEMP/obs.json'` single-quoted - double quotes and bare are handled, single quotes are not. (viii) `--observe "${{ runner.temp }}/obs.json"`, the expression form of the same directory the `path:` line already uses; reported as 'a verify step does not pass --observe', which is false of the artifact. (ix) a job head quoted with SINGLE quotes, `  'only':`, makes the whole file unreadable - `_unquoted` strips both quote characters but the two regexes that find `jobs:` and the job heads allow only `"`. That one reports 'this file runs the verifier in a shape the reader cannot see', which is at least loud. The unreadable rule also over-refuses in the other direction: a workflow that merely NAMES `scripts/verify.py` in a header or step comment without running it refuses, because the predicate is a bare substring over the whole file.

unclaimed_findings: The unreadable-file rule is the wrong shape for the job it is given. It is written as the catch-all for shapes nobody enumerated, and it is gated on `not graded` for the whole file. Every file it must protect already contains a graded verify step - that is why it is a file worth protecting - so the gate is open on exactly the files that matter. Making it per-job, or grading `steps:` lines found against steps parsed, would close construction (A) and (B) without a parser.

The three properties are read as declared values where two of them could be measured as effects. This is the AGENTS.md 6a defect one level in from where the second witness left it: the repair moved from substring-over-the-step to key-at-depth, which is a real improvement, but the value comparison is still exact-string equality against a hand-listed vocabulary. `true` is refused and `True`, `TRUE` and `${{ true }}` are not. A set membership over a lowercased, expression-unwrapped value would close all three.

`PAIR` swallows a trailing `#` comment into the value. That is the mirror of the N19 defect the repair fixed: the fix taught `mapping_at` to skip comment lines, and left a comment on a live line able to defeat the value it follows. Currently conservative, and one edit from being the same class of bug in the other direction.

The suite's protection against a blind reader is the `assertEqual([], unretained(text))` in `test_every_workflow_verify_step_retains_its_observations`, not the two counts. The comment above `assertEqual(4, graded)` says 'A reader that found nothing would satisfy every assertion above', which is true of that test in isolation and reads as though the count is what stops it. A reader that found each job as one step satisfies both counts.

The `graded` counter in that test counts `"scripts/verify.py" in step` over the RAW step, while `unretained` counts over the step with comment lines removed. So writing `# see scripts/verify.py` inside any workflow step fails the suite with 'the reader found a different number of verify steps'. Confirmed by executing it. Harmless today, misleading when it fires.

Nothing still reads the retained artifacts. The builder names this as an unrepaired residual and the second witness confirmed it; it is unchanged at this head. `if-no-files-found: error` remains the whole of the runtime enforcement, which is why the `continue-on-error` spellings in claim 4 matter more than their obscurity suggests.

The guard module is now 434 lines and holds a hand-rolled YAML reader, twenty-one test methods and a 26-line prose account of two witness sessions. The prose is genuinely useful and belongs somewhere; a test module that the size check is written not to see is not obviously that somewhere.

The first witness's observation record, committed at fa8ec9a and carried forward at this head, still declares `candidate_commit: 714337a...`, which is not an ancestor of this branch. The second witness recorded this. It is unchanged and unnoted at this head.

The seven attributed verification budget debts (documentation reader 2.536s over, tooling verdict integrity 1.864s, automation health 1.146s, operation surface page 1.076s, witness receipts 0.808s, Node Interface projection 0.763s, counted populations 0.524s) are pre-existing, attributed, non-refusing, and not this change's.
residuals: The claim as stated is overstated on both of its halves, and the second half is the material one. 'Any file it cannot read that mentions the verifier refuses outright' is not what the code does: two ordinary, valid, GitHub-accepted YAML shapes place an unretained verify step inside the repository's own verify.yml and pass the entire suite. 'Refuses every verify step that keeps only an exit code' is not true of those two, nor of a retention step carrying `continue-on-error: True` or `${{ true }}`. 'All thirteen bypasses' is true of twelve items and of one spelling of the thirteenth.

The builder's own docstring is more accurate than the claim: it declares the heredoc limit in plain words and does not assert the two clauses that fail. The overstatement is in the claim presented for witness, not in the artifact.

The repair is substantial and moves the guard forward. A per-step reader that finds keys at their own depth, refuses commented-out values, refuses `continue-on-error: true`, distinguishes a step's `if:` from one inside `with:`, accepts four previously over-refused legal spellings, and grades all four live steps under three independent defeats each, is a materially better instrument than what the second witness read. It is not the instrument the claim describes.

This reading is entirely local. It says nothing about hosted runners. Per the task the CI result on this head (18 checks, 17 success, 1 skipped) was taken as given and is not evidence I re-derived; trap T5 says a skipped required check satisfies a ruleset, so 'skipped' is not something a witness can read as passing.

I did not read any Orchestrator, Controller or builder evaluative conclusion before freezing the verdicts above. I read the two prior observation records first, as the task directed, and re-executed every bypass they reported by constructing it myself rather than reading it off the new test cases.
standing_supported: NONE for the claim as stated. BUILT -> WITNESSED is not supported, because the clause the claim leans hardest on - that an unreadable shape refuses rather than passing - is defeated by two constructions inside the repository's own verify.yml. It would be supported for this narrower claim, which I did reproduce in full: 'All four scripts/verify.py invocations in .github/workflows write their per-check Observation records, and the job that wrote each file uploads that exact file with an unconditional condition, if-no-files-found: error, and no continue-on-error spelled `true`; the guard refuses twelve of the thirteen shapes two prior witnesses executed, refuses each of the three properties deleted from each of the four live steps, and refuses a workflow or composite-action file in which it finds no verify step at all while the file names the verifier.' Restating the claim to that is the builder's to do, and so is the repair. This observation is not a settlement and not a acceptance.
judgement_items: None reaches Bdo. Every item above is engineering repair inside the concern that owns it: the reader's per-file gate, the `continue-on-error` value vocabulary, the trailing-comment handling in `PAIR`, and the single-quote asymmetry between `_unquoted` and the two head regexes. Nothing here touches product intent, naming, an external effect, a secret, a resource commitment, or destructive administration.

One question is a policy reading rather than a defect, and it is settleable below the owner seat, so it is raised as a question and not escalated: does the 300-line module ceiling bind test modules? AGENTS.md:375 states it without a carve-out; AGENTS.md:430, CONTRIBUTING.md:343 and ENGINEERING.md:226 say 'production modules'; `scripts/lint.py` implements the narrower reading. The guard module is at 434. Whichever reading holds, a load-bearing reader living where the size check cannot see it is worth the builder's attention.
overall_verdict: PARTIALLY REPRODUCED, WITH DISSENT ON THE CENTRAL CLAUSE. The retention half holds and is stronger than at either prior reading: four invocations, four --observe flags, four same-job uploads that are unconditional and refusing, 55 schema-shaped records stable across two runs, verify and lint green, all three test modules passing, and nothing unrelated changed. The refusal half does not hold as claimed. Twelve of the thirteen prior bypasses close and the twelve-mutation sweep genuinely covers all four live steps, both confirmed by mutations built here rather than read off the new cases. But the rule written to cover the shapes nobody enumerated is gated on a file having yielded no graded step at all, and every file it must protect already has one: appending to verify.yml a job whose `steps:` key carries a trailing comment, or whose `steps:` is a flow sequence, puts a bare unretained `python scripts/verify.py` in the repository's own verification workflow and passes the whole suite with `graded` still 4. Both shapes are valid YAML that a parser resolves to exactly the structure the reader expects. Alongside that, `continue-on-error: True` or `${{ true }}` still takes back the runtime refusal the repair made load-bearing, and nine legal spellings are newly over-refused. This goes back to the builder for repair inside this concern; it is not a ticket and not a settlement.
